prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Issue tracker (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "ID" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 75px
  col 2: header "Title" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 394px
  col 3: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 4: header "Assignee" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 5: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 77px
  col 6: header "Updated" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 87px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r0A: widths [96, 250, 80, 87, 98, 108] · table 720×348px · row heights [36, 60, 36, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/6 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0B: widths [96, 291, 80, 87, 82, 83] · table 720×394px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 60, 60, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/6 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0C: widths [96, 206, 80, 87, 112, 138] · table 720×394px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 83, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/6 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

log.raw: {"preferred":["r0A"],"acceptable":[],"bad":[{"design":"r0B","why":"Status is squeezed to 82px so 'In progress' breaks onto two lines, and Updated at 83px splits every ISO date after the first hyphen ('2024-' / '06-02'), damaging scanability and forcing all rows to 60px."},{"design":"r0C","why":"Title is under-allocated at 206px, forcing the longest title to three lines, while Status (112px) and especially Updated (138px) carry large dead space; the result is uneven row heights and a bloated, poorly proportioned table."}],"contrast":null,"ranges":[[96,104],[245,290],[80,90],[87,97],[98,110],[108,120]],"rationale":"The table is scanned first by ID, then by title, with severity, assignee, status, and updated acting as short categorical attributes. r0A gives Title the flexible remainder while keeping every short field at its one-line width, so only titles wrap and only to two lines. r0B breaks status and dates, and r0C overfeeds the right-hand columns while starving Title. The compact, even two-line rhythm of r0A is the best reading experience.","principles":{"general":["Allocate width by scanning role: identifiers and categorical fields need just enough for one line; free-text fields absorb the flexible remainder.","Keep dates, status labels, and other short comparison values unbroken; hyphen-splitting dates is worse than wrapping a title.","A compact table with consistent one- or two-line rows usually beats a taller table with concentrated dead space."],"specific":["Here Title is the only genuinely long free-text column, so it should receive most of the slack; Severity, Assignee, Status, and Updated are short categorical fields.","The longest title needs roughly 245px of column width to stay at two lines; at 206px it becomes three lines.","Updated needs about 108px for one-line ISO dates, and Status needs about 98px for 'In progress'."]},"tradeoffs":"A designer could give Title more width (as r0B does) to reduce title wrapping, but only by squeezing Status and Updated into broken lines; that trade is not worth it. Conversely, r0C protects the short fields but wastes width on them and creates a three-line title row.","uncertain":"The exact Title threshold between two and three lines is font- and word-break-dependent, and some designers might treat r0C as merely suboptimal rather than bad because its data remains intact."}
